items.title: ROI-Tin hit by AI stock rout despite physical market tightness: Andy Home
points: Tin, which had been riding the AI wave on the back of its use as an electronic solder, has taken a particularly hard knock after Wall Street lost $3.2 trillion in a single session on Thursday as investors feared Democrats could slow the buildout of AI data…
London Metal Exchange three-month tin has slumped from over $50,000 per metric ton to an eight-month low of $45,360 in the space of a week.
The benchmark cash-to-three-months spread was in a deep contango, with prompt tin at a discount of more than $350 per ton to three-month delivery in August.
Now, however, cash tin is commanding a $125-per-ton premium over three-month delivery, its highest premium since December.
LME registered tin stocks have trended steadily lower since June and now total just 3,885 tons, their lowest level since December last year.

points: Automotive battery makers Exide Industries and Amara Raja Energy & Mobility posted contrasting results for the September quarter (Q2FY27).
Exide’s standalone Ebitda rose nearly 54% year-on-year to ₹606 crore as revenue improved 20% to ₹5,026 crore.
In contrast, Amara saw Ebitda fall 5% year-on-year to ₹386 crore—hurt by a sharp increase in input costs such as metal alloys and sulphuric acid—even as revenue grew 13% to ₹3,843 crore.
It hiked prices of four-wheelers by about 10% and two-wheelers by 5% during January-October.
Amara Raja managed only limited price hikes — 2% in Q2 after 3% in Q1 — causing its gross margin to shrink by about 300 basis points to 29.8%.
Meanwhile, its wholly owned subsidiary, Exide Energy Solutions Ltd (EESL), commissioned a 6 GWh lithium-ion cell facility in Q2.
Both stocks have corrected 29% from their respective 52-week highs in August.
So far this calendar year, however, Exide is down just 3%, compared with a 22% drop in Amara Raja.

points: (Bloomberg) -- Australia’s regulator stopped Angas Securities Ltd. from selling two managed investment schemes, the latest in a slew of actions to prevent private credit funds offering products that don’t adequately highlight potential risks.

The interim stop orders from the Australian Securities and Investments Commission prevent the Adelaide-based firm from offering, issuing, selling, or transferring interests in the Angas Prime Income Fund and the Angas Direct Mortgage Fund, according to a…

items.title: Stowaway prevention: best practice
points: Stowaways remain a significant security and operational risk for vessels calling at ports in West Africa.
Two recent cases handled by Skuld once again highlight the persistent stowaway risk in the region and the importance of conducting thorough and systematic physical searches.
Even where professional third-party security services and trained search dogs are employed, the vessel’s own search remains a critical element of effective stowaway prevention.
Effective prevention requires strict access control, vigilant watchkeeping and thorough, vessel-specific physical searches.

Third-party security measures, including searches using trained dogs, should be regarded as an additional layer of protection and should supplement, rather than replace, the vessel’s own stowaway searches.
Recent cases and lessons learnt In the first case, in early August 2026, seven stowaways were discovered several days after the vessel’s departure, when they emerged from hiding.
The vessel had subsequently called at San Pedro, Côte d’Ivoire.
Best practices For vessels calling at ports with an elevated stowaway risk, Skuld recommends a layered approach centred on access control and systematic physical searches.

points: Caribbean countries and maritime stakeholders have developed a draft regional roadmap to advance maritime decarbonization and ensure a just transition across the region.

The initiative is expected to provide a shared framework for Caribbean countries, regional institutions, the maritime industry and development partners to advance practical projects, investment and technical cooperation.

The draft Caribbean Regional Roadmap for Maritime Decarbonization and a Just Transition (2027–2035) aims to provide a practical framework for coordinated regional action, technical cooperation and investment.

It was developed during a regional workshop held in Georgetown, Guyana (28–29 October) The event brought together representatives from maritime administrations, the Caribbean Community (CARICOM), the Caribbean Shipping Association (CSA), financial…
The workshop aimed to identify priority actions to implement the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, while safeguarding affordable shipping, regional connectivity and essential maritime services.

items.title: HPCL Struggles To Book Tankers For Hormuz Crude
points: The challenge persists even as crude supplies from the Middle East recover and more vessels resume crossings through the strategic waterway.

HPCL Chairman Vikas Kaushal said in an interview in Abu Dhabi this week that finding ships for available loading dates remains difficult, with some shipowners withdrawing even after agreeing to transport cargoes.
While the refiner has managed to secure crude supplies from the region, arranging vessels to lift cargoes from within the Persian Gulf has become a significant operational challenge.
Oil flows from the Middle East have increased in recent months, with more vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz despite Iran ramping up maritime attacks.
HPCL bought an average of about 2,40,000 barrels per day of Middle Eastern crude in 2025, according to data from energy intelligence provider Kpler.
The volume declined to 57,000 barrels per day in April 2026, when the conflict severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

items.title: Turkey’s coal dependence faces scrutiny as COP31 climate summit begins
points: Turkey’s reliance on coal is facing renewed scrutiny ahead of the COP31 climate summit, as communities affected by mining operations urge world leaders to examine the environmental damage linked to the country’s largest electricity source.
The United Nations climate conference begins Monday in Antalya and runs through November 20, with the transition toward cleaner energy among the central issues under discussion.
Residents of Ikizkoy, near the Akbelen forest in southwestern Mugla province, want delegates to visit communities affected by decades of lignite mining and the expansion of nearby coal operations.
Coal generated 34% of Turkey’s electricity last year, making the country Europe’s largest producer of coal-fired power, according to energy research group Ember.
Mining operations around Akbelen supply the Yenikoy and Kemerkoy power plants, which together generate slightly more than 2% of Turkey’s electricity.
The facilities are operated by Yenikoy-Kemerkoy Energy, a joint venture involving Turkish companies Limak and IC Ictas.
